ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Shreveport, LA tanks, piping, vessels and port equipment, done on your site. Request a UT quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Shreveport, Louisiana
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld examination at industrial sites around Shreveport and Bossier City: storage tanks, process and gas piping, pressure vessels, structural steel and the heavy equipment that serves the Red River port. Technicians are mobilized to your site with flaw detectors, thickness gauges, probes and calibration blocks, work to a written procedure, and report readings against the code you name. Request an ultrasonic testing quote and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Shreveport

Shreveport grew up on petroleum, natural gas, chemicals and iron and steel products, and it sits at the head of navigation on the Red River, where the Port of Caddo-Bossier covers roughly five thousand acres with interstate and rail access. That mix produces a steady list of ultrasonic work. Natural gas gathering, compression and treating facilities serve the Haynesville play that centers on northwest Louisiana and east Texas, and every one of them has piping, separators and bottles whose walls thin from internal corrosion. Storage tanks at terminals and process plants need floor and shell readings. Barksdale Air Force Base in Bossier City and the industrial parks around it add structural steel, support equipment and fabricated assemblies.

Typical ultrasonic jobs for this area include:

  • Wall thickness grids on aboveground tank shells and roofs, and spot readings on tank floors from the outside where access allows.
  • Thickness readings at condition monitoring locations on gas and liquid piping, including elbows, tees and dead legs where corrosion concentrates.
  • Remaining wall on pressure vessels, separators and compressor scrubbers ahead of an inspection interval decision.
  • Angle-beam examination of groove welds on new fabrication, repair welds and structural connections.
  • Thickness checks on barge-loading and port handling equipment, crane booms and pressure-containing skids.
  • Lamination checks on plate before welding, and baseline readings on new piping for the owner's records.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it misses

A transducer sends a short pulse of sound into the steel through a couplant, and the instrument displays the echoes that return. Timing a back-wall echo gives thickness. An echo that arrives early from inside the metal points to a reflector such as a lamination, a void or a planar flaw in a weld. The method sees volume, which makes it the standard answer to the question of how much wall is left, and it can size and locate planar flaws that a surface method cannot reach.

It has limits that matter on Shreveport equipment. A rough, scaled or heavily pitted surface scatters the sound and gives unstable readings, so surface preparation is part of the job. Coarse-grained cast or weld metal attenuates the beam. Very thin wall, and flaws oriented parallel to the beam, are easy to misread. Pitting is the classic trap: a gauge that sits on a high spot between pits reports a healthy wall that is not representative, so the technician scans an area and records the lowest reading instead of a single point. Ultrasonics also cannot tell you whether a flaw is cracking from fatigue or a fabrication defect without the technician reading the echo pattern and the weld geometry.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Louisiana work

The method is defined by the codes that call for it. ASME Section V Article 5 covers ultrasonic examination of materials, Article 4 covers welds, and Article 23 carries SE-797 for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement. ASTM E797 is the matching practice in general industry, and ASTM E164 covers contact examination of weldments. For weld acceptance the technician applies the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping with its Table 341.3.2, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and API 1104 for pipeline welds.

For in-service equipment, API 510, API 570 and API 653 put the inspection program under the owner's authorized inspector, who decides intervals and fitness for continued service. Atlantis supplies the examination data, not the inspector of record. At the state level, the Office of State Fire Marshal's Boiler Inspection Section administers the Louisiana boiler and pressure vessel rules and adopts the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code as the state construction code, so repair and alteration records for jurisdictional vessels need to sit comfortably beside the readings we hand over. Gas and liquid pipelines fall under PHMSA's 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, and plants with highly hazardous chemicals work under OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119, whose mechanical integrity element calls for inspection to recognized good practice.

Technique: thickness surveys and weld examination

Thickness work starts with a dual-element probe, because its separate transmit and receive crystals cope with corroded, pitted surfaces better than a single-element probe. The technician calibrates on a step block made of the same material, checks the zero and velocity, and verifies calibration again at the end. On pitted or thin wall the A-scan display is watched, not just the digital number, so a doubled echo or a premature signal is caught. Hot surfaces need a high-temperature probe and couplant, plus a temperature correction. Readings are taken at marked locations on a grid so the next survey can repeat them and the corrosion rate can be calculated.

Weld examination uses angle-beam shear wave probes, commonly at forty-five, sixty and seventy degrees, matched to the thickness and joint. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, and the technician scans both sides of the weld, from the weld face or the base metal, looking for lack of fusion, cracks, slag and porosity. Indications above the reporting level are located, evaluated for length and amplitude, and compared with the acceptance criteria. Our ultrasonic testing guide and the national UT service page go deeper into probe selection.

Who performs the work

The people who run the instruments are qualified through Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the results; an ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews reports. Under that recommended practice the employer certifies its own personnel, which is why we keep the written practice available to customers who want to audit it. Atlantis has no office in Shreveport. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and any plant orientation, badging or site safety training you require is built into the plan before they arrive. Procedures are written to the code on your purchase order and, where you have your own, we work to yours after review. See written practice development and Level III consulting for the oversight side.

What the UT report contains

A usable ultrasonic report lets someone who was not on the site understand and repeat the work. Ours identifies the component by tag or line number, the procedure and revision, the code and acceptance criteria, the instrument, probes, couplant and calibration block, and the calibration checks. It names the technician and certification level, records surface condition and temperature, and states the examination date and the extent covered.

For thickness surveys the report includes a sketch or grid with every reading, the nominal and minimum required wall where you supply them, and flags for readings under the threshold. For weld examination it lists each recordable indication with position, length, depth and amplitude, then states accept or reject against the named criteria. Calibration and reference blocks are tied to the report, so the data stays defensible when an authorized inspector, an insurer or an auditor reviews it months later.

Sizing a survey so the data is worth having

A thickness survey is only as useful as its repeatability. Before we mark a single reading we agree on the location scheme with you: how many readings per elbow, how a tank shell is divided into courses and grids, and how floor plates are numbered. Where earlier surveys exist we reuse their locations so the corrosion rate comes from like-for-like readings rather than a fresh pattern. Where they do not, the first survey becomes the baseline, and the layout is written into the report so the next technician can follow it without guessing.

Planning a UT job in Shreveport

Summers around Shreveport are hot and humid, and a steel shell in direct sun can reach temperatures where ordinary couplant dries out and standard probes wear quickly, so we plan surface temperature, probe selection and shade before the first reading. Spring storms and sustained rain bring delays on outdoor tank and pipe rack work, and winter cold snaps affect couplant and instrument performance, so schedule slack is worth building in. Plants and terminals each have orientation, permit and lockout requirements, and port-side work involves coordination with the facility on access and vessel movements.

Insulation removal, scaffolding and surface cleaning are usually the long poles in a thickness survey, so confirm who provides them. Send us the equipment list, the drawings or datasheets, the previous survey readings and the governing code. We then propose the scope, the number of readings and the format of the report. Work around planned outages is common, and an early request lets the scope be fixed before turnaround contractors crowd the site.

UT, MT or PT for your job in Shreveport

Choose the method by the question. If you need remaining wall, corrosion rate or the volume of a weld, ultrasonics is the answer. If you need to know whether a ferromagnetic weld toe or lug has a surface crack after fabrication or repair, magnetic particle inspection in Shreveport is faster and more sensitive at the surface. If the material is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy and you suspect a surface-breaking flaw, liquid penetrant testing in Shreveport is the fit. Many repair packages use two of them together: ultrasonics to confirm remaining wall and weld soundness, then a surface method on the final weld. Ask us what your code requires and we will say which method it names.

You can also read about the wider inspection services across Louisiana.

Training your own UT technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, Atlantis runs UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, and the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator lets trainees practice scanning before they touch real equipment. Your company then certifies its own staff under its written practice. For local interest in qualification, see NDT training for Shreveport.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing measure on Shreveport tanks and piping?
faq.a: It measures the remaining wall of steel by timing the echo from the back wall. Readings are taken on a marked grid or at condition monitoring locations so the owner can compare surveys over time and calculate a corrosion rate for each tank, line or vessel.

faq.q: Can you inspect welds ultrasonically, or only measure thickness?
faq.a: We do both. Thickness gauging uses dual-element probes, and weld examination uses angle-beam shear wave probes with a reference level built from side-drilled holes. Weld indications are judged against the acceptance criteria of the construction code that applies to the job.

faq.q: Do I need to prepare the surface before ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. Loose scale, paint blisters and heavy rust interfere with coupling and can make readings unstable. At minimum the contact area should be wire-brushed or ground smooth. Tell us the condition in advance and we will plan cleaning or confirm who will remove coatings and insulation.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing useful on hot equipment?
faq.a: It can be. High-temperature probes and couplant allow readings on warm surfaces, with a correction applied for temperature. Very hot lines may need to be examined for short contact periods or after cool-down, and we agree the limits with the owner before the work.

faq.q: Which codes do you use for UT acceptance?
faq.a: We use whatever the construction code or owner specification names, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1, ASME B31.3, AWS D1.1 or API 1104 for welds, with ASME Section V Article 4 or Article 5 governing the technique. For thickness there is usually a minimum required wall rather than a flaw criterion.

faq.q: Do you act as the API authorized inspector?
faq.a: No. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record and decides intervals and fitness for service. Atlantis supplies the ultrasonic data, calibration records and the report that inspector relies on.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Shreveport?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and technicians are mobilized to your Shreveport or Bossier City site for the agreed scope. Orientation, badging and access requirements are planned with you before anyone travels.

faq.q: What documents should I send for a UT quote?
faq.a: Send the equipment list or line list, the governing code, drawings or datasheets, nominal and minimum wall values, access constraints and any earlier thickness data. With that we can propose the scope, the number of locations and the report format. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can my own staff learn ultrasonic testing through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a Practical NDT simulator for practice. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own personnel, using its written practice, once the training and experience requirements are met.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Shreveport, LA
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing of Shreveport, LA welds, lugs, cranes and gas facility steel, on your site. Request an MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Shreveport, Louisiana
mt.html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) finds surface cracks and other surface-breaking flaws in carbon and low-alloy steel, and Atlantis NDT carries it out at industrial sites in the Shreveport and Bossier City area. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, terminal, yard or shop with yokes, particles, a light meter and field indicators, and report indications against the code you name. Typical targets are weld toes, lugs, crane parts, nozzle attachments and repair excavations. Ask for a magnetic particle quote; a reply comes within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used around Shreveport

Steel dominates the Shreveport industrial landscape. The city has long been a center for petroleum, natural gas, chemicals and iron and steel products, and the Port of Caddo-Bossier at the head of the Red River navigation handles bulk and industrial cargo in a large industrial park. Gas gathering and compression sites supporting the Haynesville play, tank terminals, rail-served fabrication shops and the maintenance operations around Barksdale Air Force Base all weld, lift and repair carbon steel.

Mag particle jobs that come up in this area:

  • Weld toes on pressure vessel attachments, saddles and nozzle reinforcement pads, examined after fabrication or repair.
  • Crack checks at the ends of repair grinds on piping and tanks, before welding resumes.
  • Lifting lugs, pad eyes, shackles and spreader bars on port and construction cranes.
  • Gas compressor skids, frames and supports, examined after modification or a vibration problem.
  • Structural connections on pipe racks, platforms and stairways at process and gas facilities.
  • Trailers, truck-mounted equipment and heavy-duty fabricated parts where fatigue cracks start at welds.

How the method works, and what it cannot see

The technician magnetizes the part. A crack or similar discontinuity that interrupts the magnetic field causes flux to leak from the surface, and iron particles dusted or sprayed on the part gather there, forming a visible line that outlines the flaw. The method is fast, sensitive to tight cracks that penetrant testing might miss under paint residue or smeared metal, and does not demand a perfectly clean surface.

The limits are firm. The material must be ferromagnetic: carbon steel and most low-alloy steels respond, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and brass do not. Only surface and slightly subsurface discontinuities are detected, and sensitivity drops quickly with depth. The method says nothing about wall thickness or deep internal flaws. Flaws are only revealed when they lie across the magnetic field, which is why the field direction is the core technical decision. A crack running parallel to the flux lines can be missed entirely, so a second pass at roughly ninety degrees to the first is required. Thick coatings reduce sensitivity and may need to be removed or demonstrated acceptable.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply

ASME Section V Article 7 sets the technique requirements, and ASTM E709 is the guide for the method with ASTM E1444 as the practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 defines MT methods and acceptance for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 cover process piping, and AWS D1.1 addresses structural steel welds. For in-service work, API 510, 570 and 653 place decisions with the owner's authorized inspector; Atlantis performs the examination and reports the indications that inspector evaluates.

Louisiana adds a layer. The Office of State Fire Marshal's Boiler Inspection Section administers the state's boiler and pressure vessel rules and adopts the ASME Code as the state's construction code, with inspection done by the state or by licensed insurers' inspectors holding a National Board commission. Repairs to jurisdictional vessels follow the National Board Inspection Code. Plants subject to OSHA's process safety management standard in 29 CFR 1910.119 also expect mechanical integrity records that tie to recognized good engineering practice. We write the report so it supports whichever record trail applies.

Technique: yokes, particles and field indicators

For most field work we use an electromagnetic yoke. The Article 7 requirement is that an AC yoke lift at least ten pounds at the pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least forty pounds. We verify that with a test weight before use. Dry visible powder suits warm, rough surfaces such as weld metal; wet visible or fluorescent particles give the highest sensitivity on smooth parts and are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, with the intensity and ambient light checked by meter. Contrast paint provides a background when visible particles are used on dark surfaces.

Technicians verify field strength and direction with a pie gauge or a shim indicator, apply the particles while the field is on, and examine in two directions. For critical welds, or on thick sections, prods or a coil may be specified. Afterward, residual magnetism is checked and the part is demagnetized when it would interfere with later welding, machining or service, for example in bearing seats or near instruments. Read the complete guide to magnetic particle testing or the Article 7 explainer for more on the requirements.

Who does the work, and under what authority

Atlantis technicians are qualified under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians set up and calibrate the equipment, perform the examination and interpret indications; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Because SNT-TC-1A is employer-based, the company that employs the technician certifies them, which is why we make the written practice available for review. Atlantis has no office in Shreveport. Technicians are mobilized to your site, and we plan travel, orientation and access with you ahead of the work. Our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is an ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and procedure approval sits with Level III oversight. For a customer procedure review, see Level III consulting.

What the magnetic particle report records

The report names the component and its location, the procedure and revision, the code and acceptance criteria, and the technique used: yoke type, particle type, wet or dry, color, and the directions examined. It records the lifting-power check, the light meter reading for fluorescent work, surface condition and temperature, and the examination date. The technician and certification level are listed.

Every recordable indication appears with its position, orientation and length, plus a sketch or photograph where useful, and a clear accept or reject against the named criteria. If a flaw is ground out, the follow-up examination of the excavation is recorded the same way. The result is a document that stands up when an authorized inspector, an insurer or a customer auditor asks how a repair was verified.

Common problems we watch for on mag particle jobs

Most poor magnetic particle results trace back to a handful of causes, and a careful technician checks for each one before accepting a clean result. Poor contact between yoke legs and a rough or painted weld reduces flux in the part, so surface condition is inspected first. A yoke used at the wrong pole spacing delivers less field than the lift test assumed. Particles applied after the field is switched off, or applied too heavily, either wash off the indication or bury it. Non-relevant indications, such as those at a sharp change of section or the edge of a magnetic writing mark, are a common source of confusion and have to be separated from true flaws by re-examination, often after light dressing of the surface.

The same discipline applies to repair work. When a crack is ground out, the excavation is re-examined before welding to prove the flaw is gone, and again after welding and any required post-weld heat treatment, since some cracks do not appear until the weld has cooled. Recording each step gives the owner and the authorized inspector a clear chain from defect to repair to final acceptance.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Shreveport

Weather is a real factor on outdoor steel. Midsummer heat can push a shell past the temperature where wet particles dry too fast and carrier liquid evaporates, and humid air complicates surface cleaning and drying of particle suspensions. Spring storms and winter cold bring their own constraints, so a covered work area or schedule flexibility helps. For fluorescent work, UV-A examination needs darkness or a tent, which can be difficult in full sun.

Tell us the base metal, coating and weld type, the code, and how much of each weld needs examination. Provide access, power if needed and any hot work or confined space permits. Plant orientation and badging are common at gas and process facilities in the area, and port-side sites add their own access routines. Early notice lets us line up the right equipment, which is especially useful for turnaround and shutdown windows when crews are scarce.

MT, PT or UT for your Shreveport job

Magnetic particle inspection is the first choice for surface cracks in carbon steel welds. If the part is stainless or aluminum, or the surface is non-magnetic, use liquid penetrant testing in Shreveport. If you need wall thickness, corrosion rate or a volumetric examination of a weld, ultrasonic testing in Shreveport is the fit. Repair packages often combine methods. Read MT versus PT compared for a quick decision guide, or see the national magnetic particle testing page and the Louisiana inspection services hub.

Training your own MT technicians

For in-house capability, Atlantis offers MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training. Your company certifies its own personnel under its written practice. Local readers can also look at NDT training for Shreveport, and check SNT-TC-1A eligibility to see what experience hours apply.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on?
faq.a: Ferromagnetic materials only, which in practice means carbon steel and most alloy steels. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or copper alloys, which are not attracted to a magnet. For those materials, liquid penetrant testing is the usual surface method.

faq.q: Is mag particle testing able to find subsurface cracks?
faq.a: It can reveal flaws just under the surface, but sensitivity falls quickly with depth. Deep internal flaws are outside the method. If you need to find internal weld flaws or measure remaining wall, ultrasonic testing is the appropriate method.

faq.q: Why are two directions of magnetization required?
faq.a: A flaw shows only when it crosses the magnetic field. A crack parallel to the field lines can be missed, so the part is examined with the field in two directions at roughly right angles. That is how the code makes sure cracks in any orientation are caught.

faq.q: Do you use wet or dry magnetic particles?
faq.a: We choose by the job. Dry visible powder suits rough, warm weld surfaces. Wet particles, visible or fluorescent, give higher sensitivity on smooth surfaces and are common for critical welds. The procedure states the choice and the code or owner specification can require one.

faq.q: Does paint or coating need to be removed before MT?
faq.a: Thin, tight coatings can sometimes remain if the procedure demonstrates that sensitivity is still adequate. Thick or flaking coatings usually have to be removed. We confirm the limit with a demonstration on a representative sample before examining the real part.

faq.q: When is demagnetization needed after inspection?
faq.a: When residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, instruments or service, such as arc blow during welding or particles clinging to bearing surfaces. The technician checks the residual field and demagnetizes if it exceeds the limit set in the procedure.

faq.q: Can you do magnetic particle inspection at night or during a shutdown?
faq.a: We can schedule technicians around your outage windows. Fluorescent examination actually benefits from darkness. Tell us your shutdown schedule early so that equipment and personnel are lined up. We do not promise a specific arrival time before the scope is agreed.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Shreveport office or lab?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and technicians travel to your Shreveport or Bossier City site. Orientation, badging, power and access are planned with you before the work starts.

faq.q: Who certifies Atlantis technicians for MT?
faq.a: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel. Atlantis qualifies technicians under its written practice, with Level II performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. We can share that written practice for audit.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant in Shreveport, LA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection of stainless, aluminum and alloy welds in Shreveport, LA, done on your site. Request a PT quote today.
pt.h1: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Shreveport, Louisiana
pt.html:
Liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection or PT, reveals cracks, laps, porosity and other flaws that open to the surface of a part, and it works on metals that magnetic methods cannot handle. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to plants, terminals and fabrication sites in the Shreveport and Bossier City area to examine stainless steel piping, aluminum components, nonferrous welds and cast or forged parts. Ask for a penetrant testing quote; a reply comes within one business day.

Where dye penetrant inspection fits in Shreveport

Shreveport's industrial economy covers petroleum, natural gas, chemicals and metal products, and its port on the Red River serves manufacturers and distributors. That variety means a lot of material that is not carbon steel. Chemical and gas processing plants use stainless and alloy piping where chloride cracking and fatigue are credible damage mechanisms. Fabrication shops weld stainless skids and aluminum structures. Barksdale Air Force Base and the surrounding supply chain use alloy and light-metal hardware that needs surface checks.

Examples of penetrant work in this area:

  • Root and cap passes on stainless steel and alloy process piping, examined as the weld is completed.
  • Weld repairs on aluminum equipment, trailers and structural assemblies.
  • Castings, valve bodies and pump casings checked for surface porosity and cracks.
  • Heat exchanger and vessel nozzle welds in stainless or duplex materials.
  • Carbon steel welds where magnetic inspection is impractical because of geometry or access.
  • Final examination of ground-out areas after a defect is removed, to prove no crack remains.

What penetrant testing detects and where it stops

A visible or fluorescent liquid is applied to a clean surface and given time to enter any opening. The excess is removed, a developer is applied, and the developer draws liquid back out of the flaw, producing a bleed-out that is far larger and easier to see than the flaw itself. The method works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not, and is sensitive to fine surface-breaking cracks.

Its limit is defined by its name: the flaw must be open to the surface. A crack closed by smeared metal from grinding, blasting or machining will not take up penetrant, and heavy paint, oil, scale or weld spatter that fills a flaw hides it. Rough or porous surfaces create broad background bleed-out that masks real indications. PT says nothing about flaws beneath the surface or about wall thickness. That is why the cleaning step is treated as part of the examination, and why mechanical cleaning before inspection is restricted in many procedures: abrasive blasting and wire brushing can peen the surface closed.

Codes and acceptance criteria for penetrant work

ASME Section V Article 6 defines the technique requirements, with ASTM E165 as the general industry practice. Acceptance comes from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 covers PT methods and acceptance for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 applies to process piping, and ASME B31.1 governs power piping. AWS D1.1 and AWS D1.6 apply to structural carbon steel and stainless steel respectively, and the owner may layer on its own specification.

For in-service equipment under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector makes the decisions about acceptance and repair. We supply the indications and the record. In Louisiana, the Office of State Fire Marshal's Boiler Inspection Section administers the boiler and pressure vessel rules, and repairs to jurisdictional equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code, so the penetrant record often becomes part of a repair package. For plants covered by OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119, penetrant results feed the mechanical integrity file. Our Article 6 explainer walks through the technique requirements.

Technique: from cleaning to final interpretation

The sequence is controlled by the procedure. The surface is cleaned of oil, grease, scale and coating and then dried. Penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion and left to dwell for the time the procedure sets, which depends on the material, the expected flaw and the temperature. Excess is removed according to the method: water washable, solvent removable or post-emulsifiable. Developer is applied thinly and evenly, then given development time before interpretation.

Type I fluorescent penetrants are examined under UV-A light in darkness and give the highest sensitivity; Type II visible dye penetrants, usually red, are examined under white light and suit field work where a dark area is impractical. The solvent-removable visible method is the common field choice at plants. The technician evaluates indications within the window the procedure allows, distinguishes relevant flaws from nonrelevant bleed-out from geometry, and retests when an indication is doubtful. Temperature matters: the Article 6 standard range is a limited window around ambient shop conditions, and work outside it requires a procedure qualified for the actual temperature, a point we check before starting. See the MT versus PT comparison for guidance on method choice.

Who performs penetrant testing for Atlantis

Penetrant technicians work under Atlantis's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform the examination and interpret indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. Because the employer certifies its own people under that recommended practice, we are open about the written practice and happy to let customers audit it. Atlantis has no office in Shreveport. Technicians are mobilized to your site, and orientation, badging and access are agreed with you before travel. Where your site has its own procedure, we review it and work to it. See written practice development for related services.

What the penetrant testing report includes

The report identifies the component, material, weld or area examined, the procedure and revision, and the acceptance criteria. It lists the penetrant system by type, method and manufacturer, the cleaner and developer, dwell and development times, and the surface and ambient temperature. The technician name and level appear, along with the date and extent of examination.

Indications are recorded with location, shape and size, whether linear or rounded, and relevant or nonrelevant status, with a photograph or sketch where it helps. Each is marked accept or reject against the named criteria. Where a repair follows, the re-examination after grinding or welding is reported the same way. The record can be dropped straight into a repair package or a quality file.

Choosing the penetrant system for the job

Penetrant systems are classified by the dye (visible or fluorescent) and by how the excess is removed, and the choice changes sensitivity, speed and cost of cleanup. Water-washable systems are quick on large, rough parts such as castings but can over-wash shallow flaws. Solvent-removable systems are slower and more controlled, which is why they dominate field inspection of welds. Post-emulsifiable systems give high sensitivity on critical parts but need an extra emulsification step with tight timing. The procedure fixes the system, and the owner or construction code may restrict it further, for example by capping halogen and sulfur content on penetrant materials used on stainless steel and nickel alloys, because those elements can attack the metal if they are left behind.

Before we begin we verify the materials against their batch certificates, check the developer for contamination, and run a comparator or reference panel to confirm that the system reveals fine cracks at the temperature of the day. If the panel shows weak indications, the batch or the process is corrected before any production part is examined.

Recording difficult indications

Not every bleed-out is a flaw. Scratches, tool marks, weld ripple and sharp transitions trap penetrant and can look like cracks. A technician distinguishes them by examining the shape, the pattern of the bleed-out as developer dries, and the location relative to the weld, and by wiping the spot, reapplying developer and re-examining. Linear indications at the weld toe or a crater are treated as potential cracks, and rounded indications are classified by size against the acceptance criteria. Where an indication is borderline, the report says so and the owner or Level III decides whether a further look, a light dressing, or a different method is appropriate.

Planning a penetrant job in Shreveport

Penetrant is temperature sensitive, and Shreveport swings between humid heat and winter cold. A steel surface in summer sun can run well above the standard window and flash off solvent cleaner and penetrant, while a cold morning can slow the dwell and make developer coat unevenly. If the surface falls outside the range, we either shade or warm the part to bring it back, or use a procedure qualified for the actual temperature. Humidity affects drying times and developer behavior, and rain stops outdoor work.

Plan for cleaning. Surface preparation often takes longer than the examination, and chemicals used for cleaning need the plant's approval and ventilation in confined spaces. Tell us about the material, the coatings, the weld type and the code, and about any chloride limits on penetrant materials for stainless steel, which many owners specify. Plant orientation and badging are common, and port-side facilities coordinate access with their operators. Early notice makes it easier to fit outage windows.

faq.q: What kinds of flaws does dye penetrant inspection find?
faq.a: It finds flaws that are open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, seams and porosity. It cannot find flaws that are fully below the surface, and it will not detect cracks that have been closed by smeared metal.

faq.q: Does penetrant testing work on stainless steel and aluminum parts?
faq.a: Yes. Unlike magnetic particle inspection, penetrant testing works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not. That makes it the usual surface method for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and many castings. Owners often set chloride and sulfur limits on penetrant materials for stainless.

faq.q: Why does surface cleaning matter so much for PT?
faq.a: Penetrant must enter the flaw. Oil, scale, paint, weld spatter or smeared metal can block it and hide a real crack. Cleaning is therefore treated as part of the examination, and mechanical methods such as blasting that can peen the surface closed are usually restricted.

faq.q: What temperatures can penetrant testing be done at?
faq.a: The standard range under ASME Section V is a moderate window around ambient. Hot or cold surfaces outside it need a procedure qualified for that temperature, or the part must be brought into range. We check surface temperature before every examination.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye, usually red against a white developer, is seen in normal light and suits the field. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light in darkness and is more sensitive. The procedure or code specifies which method may be used.

faq.q: How long does penetrant need to dwell before it is removed?
faq.a: The dwell time is set by the procedure and depends on the material, the type of flaw expected and the temperature. It is not a quick wipe. Cutting the dwell short reduces sensitivity, so technicians use a timer and record the time in the report.

faq.q: Do you act as the owner's authorized inspector for penetrant work?
faq.a: No. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector makes the acceptance and repair decisions. Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and reports the indications and technique so that inspector can decide.
